title: Prototypes Sized to the Question
intro: Name the question first. Then build the cheapest prototype that answers it.

learn.title: What it tests
learn.text:
**Role:** what it does in someone’s life.
**Look and feel:** what it’s like to use.
**Implementation:** whether it can work.
**Integration:** all three, built last.

try.q: A storyboard of a new service tests mostly:
try.explain: What it does in someone’s life.

learn.title: Fidelity isn’t completeness
learn.text:
Detail and polish don’t show how settled a design is.

A rough sketch can answer a role question; a polished mockup can hide that nobody knows how it works.

options: Which design tool to build it in and share it from

learn.title: Habits
learn.text:
Build **several**, with different tools, and throw them away.
Know your audience.
**Say what it doesn’t answer.**

try.q: Why say what a prototype doesn’t answer?
options: Prototypes don’t explain their own purpose
It avoids version-control conflicts between files
try.explain: Otherwise people judge it on the wrong things.

learn.title: Types for testing ideas
learn.text:
**Paper:** flow and role.
**Clickable:** navigation.
**Realistic façade:** a whole idea in days.
**Single-feature:** real use.
**Wizard of Oz:** a person behind the curtain.

try.q: A service looks automated but a person does the work. This is:

test.q: A technical spike on data performance tests:
test.explain: Whether and how it can work.

options: After focused ones answer their questions
Instead of running any user tests at all
Only for marketing demos and sales pitches to clients
test.explain: They are slow and hard to build.

test.q: Testing comprehension with a beautiful mockup invites:
test.explain: Polish pulls attention to the surface.

test.q: In a design sprint, Thursday’s prototype is:
options: A working production build with real data

test.q: How many prototypes should you build?
What decides a prototype’s audience fit?
options: Who will see it and what they decide
The design tool licence your company has bought
test.explain: A customer test and a leadership pitch differ.
